claim: Transient pharmacological silencing of the auditory cortex using the GABA-A agonist muscimol abolishes the ability of rodents to perform a sound detection task.
source: Transient pharmacological silencing of the auditory cortex using the GABA-A agonist muscimol has been shown to abolish the ability of rodents (Talwar et al., 2001), including head-fixed mice (Li et al., 2017), to perform a sound detection task
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Talwar et al., 2001; Li et al., 2017)

claim: Optogenetic suppression of cortical activity by photoactivating ChR2-expressing inhibitory neurons in Gad2-IRES-cre mice significantly impaired sound detection performance.
source: We found that optogenetic suppression of cortical activity by photoactivating ChR2-expressing inhibitory neurons in Gad2-IRES-cre mice (Lohse et al., 2020) also significantly impaired sound detection performance (Figure 1B and C)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C, and references a citation (Lohse et al., 2020)

claim: Bilateral lesions of the auditory cortex leave sound detection performance intact in mice.
source: Several recent studies have shown that in contrast to the disruptive effects of transient silencing, cortical lesions leave performance in some sensory tasks intact (Hong et al., 2018; Ceballo et al., 2019; O'Sullivan et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent studies (Hong et al., 2018; Ceballo et al., 2019; O'Sullivan et al., 2019)

claim: There was no difference between lesioned and non-lesioned mice in their learning speed for the click detection task.
source: There was no difference between lesioned and non-lesioned mice in their learning speed (Figure 3A, p>0.05, mixed-design ANOVAs)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (p>0.05, mixed-design ANOVAs) and data shown in Figure 3A

claim: There was no difference between lesioned and non-lesioned mice in their psychometric functions for the click detection task.
source: or psychometric functions (Figure 3B, p>0.05, mixed-design ANOVA)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (p>0.05, mixed-design ANOVA) and data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Most corticocollicular neurons project ipsilaterally, with a substantial proportion also sending axons to the contralateral midbrain.
source: Most corticocollicular neurons project ipsilaterally, with a substantial proportion also sending axons to the contralateral midbrain (Stebbings et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stebbings et al., 2014

claim: The majority of corticocollicular neurons are found in the temporal cortex, and overwhelmingly in the auditory fields.
source: The majority of corticocollicular neurons are found in the temporal cortex, and overwhelmingly in the auditory fields, while a small fraction populates adjacent areas, such as the temporal association area (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: AAV1.hSyn.Cre.WPRE is a virus with anterograde transsynaptic spread properties.
source: More specifically, we injected AAV1.hSyn.Cre.WPRE, a virus with anterograde transsynaptic spread properties (Zingg et al., 2017), into the right auditory cortex
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zingg et al., 2017

claim: Close to half (1272/2649) of all corticorecipient IC neurons showed a statistically significant difference in response magnitude between hit and miss trials.
source: Indeed, close to half (1272/2649) of all neurons showed a statistically significant difference in response magnitude between hit and miss trials
evidence: The claim is supported by specific numerical data from the analysis

claim: Only a small fraction (97/2649) of corticorecipient IC neurons exhibited a significant response to the sound.
source: while only a small fraction (97/2649) exhibited a significant response to the sound.
evidence: The claim is supported by specific numerical data from the analysis

claim: The activity of most corticorecipient IC neurons contained information beyond the physical properties of the stimulus.
source: This suggests that the activity of the majority of neurons in the recorded population contained information beyond the physical properties of the stimulus.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the clustering analysis showing distinct activity patterns for hit vs miss trials

claim: Lick-related sounds are estimated to be just 12 dB SPL.
source: Given that licking causes self-generated sounds, IC neurons could, in principle, respond to the sound of licking. However, given how quiet these are - estimated to be just 12 dB SPL (Singla et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Singla et al., 2017

claim: Much of the response to lick-related sounds is already canceled out at the level of the cochlear nucleus.
source: and that much of the response to such lick-related sounds is already canceled out at the level of the cochlear nucleus (Singla et al., 2017; but see Shaheen et al., 2021)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Singla et al., 2017 and Shaheen et al., 2021

claim: The average model performance was significantly above baseline in classifying hit vs miss trials in both lesioned and non-lesioned mice.
source: In both lesioned and non-lesioned mice, the average model performance was significantly above baseline in classifying hit vs miss trials (p<0.05, one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test or paired t-test with Bonferroni correction, Figure 6A)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (p<0.05) and data shown in Figure 6A

claim: The model performance in non-lesioned mice was significantly better than that in lesioned mice.
source: Additionally, the model performance in non-lesioned mice was significantly better than that in lesioned mice (p<0.05, one-sided Mann-Whitney U test or t-test with Bonferroni correction, Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (p<0.05) and data shown in Figure 6A

claim: The difference in decoding performance between lesioned and non-lesioned mice was not the result of the difference in the number of neurons recorded.
source: This difference in the decoding performance was not the result of the difference in the number of neurons between non-lesioned and lesioned mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2

claim: Four of the seven lesioned animals had (near-)complete lesions, meaning that all or an estimated ~95% of the auditory cortex had been lesioned.
source: Four of the seven lesioned animals had '(near-)complete' lesions, meaning that all (Figure 2) or an estimated ~95% (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) of the auditory cortex had been lesioned
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: The average decoding performance for mice with (near-)complete lesions was significantly better than that measured for mice with partial lesions.
source: This revealed that the average decoding performance for mice with (near-)complete lesions was significantly better than that measured for mice with partial lesions.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of decoding performance between groups

claim: The decoding performance in mice with (near-)complete lesions was largely indistinguishable from that in mice with an intact auditory cortex.
source: Additionally, the decoding performance in mice with (near-)complete lesions was largely indistinguishable from that in mice with an intact auditory cortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of decoding performance data

claim: Decoding accuracy was better than baseline even before stimulus onset.
source: Remarkably, decoding accuracy was better than baseline even before stimulus onset.
evidence: The claim is supported by decoding analysis results shown in Figure 6

claim: Changes in arousal or motivation can alter both the probability that an upcoming stimulus is detected and the activity of neurons in the network.
source: For instance, changes in arousal or motivation can alter both the probability that an upcoming stimulus is detected and the activity of neurons in the network (Lee and Dan, 2012; McGinley et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lee and Dan, 2012 and McGinley et al., 2015

claim: Average lick rates approximated the inter-trial interval distribution, suggesting that mice learned to adapt their behavior to this distribution and anticipate the timing of upcoming stimuli.
source: Nevertheless, spontaneous licks did not occur at random times during the peri-catch trial periods following hit trials. Instead, average lick rates approximated the inter-trial interval distribution (Figure 6—figure supplement 4A–D), suggesting that mice learned to adapt their behavior to this distribution and anticipate the timing of upcoming stimuli
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4A–D and inference from the observed pattern

claim: The auditory cortex is considered crucial for the integration of acoustic and contextual information.
source: The auditory cortex is considered crucial for the integration of acoustic and contextual information and is thought to share the resulting representations with subcortical auditory structures via its vast descending projections.
evidence: The claim represents established scientific consensus about the role of auditory cortex

claim: Descending projections often outnumber their feedforward counterparts.
source: The fact that descending projections often outnumber their feedforward counterparts (Sherman, 2007) attests to their likely importance for brain function.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sherman, 2007

claim: The descending projections of the auditory cortex target all major subcortical stations of the auditory pathway and are among the largest pathways of the brain.
source: The descending projections of the auditory cortex target all major subcortical stations of the auditory pathway and are among the largest pathways of the brain (Winer, 2005; Bajo and King, 2013; Antunes and Malmierca, 2021)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Winer, 2005; Bajo and King, 2013; Antunes and Malmierca, 2021

claim: The inferior colliculus is an obligatory midbrain relay for nearly all ascending auditory input.
source: One of their main targets is the inferior colliculus (IC), an obligatory midbrain relay for nearly all ascending auditory input.
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge about the auditory pathway

claim: The corticocollicular projection primarily terminates in the non-lemniscal shell of the IC.
source: The corticocollicular projection primarily terminates in the non-lemniscal shell of the IC.
evidence: The claim represents established anatomical knowledge

claim: The projection from the auditory cortex to the midbrain was identified almost a century ago.
source: The projection from the auditory cortex to the midbrain was identified almost a century ago (Mettler, 1935)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mettler, 1935

claim: Manipulating the activity of descending projection neurons can alter the collicular representations of multiple sound features.
source: decades of research have since demonstrated that manipulating the activity of descending projection neurons can alter the collicular representations of multiple sound features, influence adaptive plasticity and perceptual learning, and even trigger an innate flight response (Suga, 2008; Nakamoto et al., 2008; Bajo et al., 2010; Xiong et al., 2015; Blackwell et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Suga, 2008; Nakamoto et al., 2008; Bajo et al., 2010; Xiong et al., 2015; Blackwell et al., 2020)

claim: Behavior, cognition, and brain state can strongly influence activity in the sensory pathways.
source: Indeed, recordings in awake animals have shown that behavior, cognition, and brain state can strongly influence activity in the sensory pathways (Schneider and Mooney, 2018; McCormick et al., 2020; Parker et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schneider and Mooney, 2018; McCormick et al., 2020; Parker et al., 2020

claim: Contextual influences appear particularly strong in the cortex.
source: Consistent with a hierarchical view of sensory processing in which neurons at higher levels carry progressively more complex representations of the world, such contextual influences appear particularly strong in the cortex (Stringer et al., 2019; Musall et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Stringer et al., 2019; Musall et al., 2019

claim: Non-acoustic and contextual variables can alter sensory processing at subcortical levels, including the IC and particularly its shell.
source: Nevertheless, non-acoustic and contextual variables can also alter sensory processing at subcortical levels, including the IC and particularly its shell (Metzger et al., 2006; Gruters and Groh, 2012; Chen and Song, 2019; Yang et al., 2020; Parras et al., 2017; Saderi et al., 2021; Shaheen et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Metzger et al., 2006; Gruters and Groh, 2012; Chen and Song, 2019; Yang et al., 2020; Parras et al., 2017; Saderi et al., 2021; Shaheen et al., 2021)

claim: Auditory corticocollicular axons terminate predominantly in the shell of the IC.
source: Auditory corticocollicular axons terminate predominantly in the shell of the IC (Stebbings et al., 2014; Bajo and King, 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Stebbings et al., 2014; Bajo and King, 2013

claim: The strongest effects of cortical manipulations have been reported in the shell region of the IC.
source: and the strongest effects of cortical manipulations have been reported in this region (Nakamoto et al., 2008; Vila et al., 2019; Blackwell et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nakamoto et al., 2008; Vila et al., 2019; Blackwell et al., 2020

claim: Effects of cortical manipulations on IC can be subtle or undetectable, especially when optogenetic silencing is used.
source: However, these effects can be subtle (Cruces-Solís et al., 2018; Vila et al., 2019) or undetectable, especially when optogenetic silencing is used (Blackwell et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cruces-Solís et al., 2018; Vila et al., 2019; Blackwell et al., 2020

claim: The recordings from corticorecipient neurons in the IC are consistent with previous studies demonstrating that neural representations of behavioral variables can be found in the auditory midbrain.
source: Our recordings from corticorecipient neurons in the IC are consistent with previous studies demonstrating that neural representations of behavioral variables can be found in the auditory midbrain (Ruth et al., 1974; Nienhuis and Olds, 1978; Metzger et al., 2006; Gruters and Groh, 2012; Chen and Song, 2019; Yang et al., 2020; Saderi et al., 2021; De Franceschi and Barkat, 2021; Shaheen et al., 2021; Quass et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies

claim: The activity of most IC neurons was facilitated and about a third were suppressed during the sound detection task.
source: In keeping with responses recorded in the auditory cortex (Francis et al., 2018; De Franceschi and Barkat, 2021) and IC (Chen and Song, 2019; Yang et al., 2020; De Franceschi and Barkat, 2021) of behaving mice, we found that the activity of most neurons was facilitated and about a third were suppressed during the sound detection task.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study and citations to previous work (Francis et al., 2018; De Franceschi and Barkat, 2021; Chen and Song, 2019; Yang et al., 2020)

claim: Simple auditory skills, including the ability of freely moving rats to detect sounds, are unaffected by the removal of the auditory cortex.
source: In keeping with our findings, numerous studies (reviewed in e.g. Pickles, 1988; Buser and Imbert, 1992) have shown that simple auditory skills, including the ability of freely moving rats to detect sounds (Kelly, 1970), are unaffected by the removal of the auditory cortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to reviews (Pickles, 1988; Buser and Imbert, 1992) and a specific study (Kelly, 1970)

claim: Transient pharmacological silencing of the auditory cortex in freely moving rats completely abolishes sound detection.
source: However, transient pharmacological silencing of the auditory cortex in freely moving rats (Talwar et al., 2001), as well as head-fixed mice (Li et al., 2017), completely abolishes sound detection
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Talwar et al., 2001 and Li et al., 2017

claim: Trained mice achieve pre-lesion performance levels on simple auditory discrimination or somatosensory detection tasks suddenly and within 48 hr following cortical ablation.
source: Although our results cannot speak directly to the question of whether the preservation of sound detection without auditory cortex reflects a rewiring or repurposing of circuits in the brain, this seems unlikely given that other studies have shown that trained mice achieve pre-lesion performance levels on simple auditory discrimination (Ceballo et al., 2019; O'Sullivan et al., 2019) or somatosensory detection (Hong et al., 2018) tasks suddenly and within 48 hr following cortical ablation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ceballo et al., 2019; O'Sullivan et al., 2019; Hong et al., 2018

claim: Synaptic scaling is a process that has been suggested to take up to 48 hr.
source: In this scenario, normal operation would resume once synaptic scaling (Keck et al., 2013) had homeostatically restored normal activity in these structures, a process that has been suggested to take up to 48 hr
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Keck et al., 2013

claim: Smaller lesions can have a more disruptive effect than larger, more complete lesions, in that the time it takes mice to learn a whisker-dependent sensory detection task is anticorrelated with the size of their somatosensory cortex lesion.
source: While this finding is somewhat counterintuitive and is based on only three mice with partial lesions, it has been observed before that smaller lesions can have a more disruptive effect than larger, more complete lesions, in that the time it takes mice to learn a whisker-dependent sensory detection task is anticorrelated with the size of their somatosensory cortex lesion (Hong et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hong et al., 2018

claim: Non-acoustic sensory input can reach the IC via brainstem nuclei.
source: Additional non-acoustic sensory input can reach the IC via brainstem nuclei (Lesicko et al., 2016; Shore and Zhou, 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lesicko et al., 2016; Shore and Zhou, 2006

claim: Non-acoustic sensory input can reach the IC via the superior colliculus.
source: and the superior colliculus (Chen et al., 2018; Coleman and Clerici, 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2018; Coleman and Clerici, 1987

claim: Motor signals may reach the IC via the substantia nigra.
source: The latter, together with input from the substantia nigra (Olaźabal and Moore, 1989)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Olaźabal and Moore, 1989

claim: Motor signals may reach the IC via the globus pallidus.
source: and the globus pallidus (Moriizumi and Hattori, 1991) may also be a source of motor signals
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Moriizumi and Hattori, 1991

claim: State changes may impact on the IC via inputs from neuromodulatory structures, including the locus coeruleus and the subparafascicular, dorsal raphe and tegmental nuclei.
source: while state changes may impact on the IC via inputs from neuromodulatory structures, including the locus coeruleus and the subparafascicular, dorsal raphe and tegmental nuclei (Chen and Song, 2019, Liu et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen and Song, 2019, Liu et al., 2023

claim: IC neurons show task-related activity in the absence of auditory cortical input.
source: While modulation of IC activity by this descending projection has been implicated in various functions, most notably in the plasticity of auditory processing, we have shown in mice performing a sound detection task that IC neurons show task-related activity in the absence of auditory cortical input.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data from the study showing similar activity patterns in lesioned and non-lesioned mice

claim: Subcortical auditory structures have access to a wealth of non-acoustic information independently of the auditory cortex.
source: Surprisingly, this was also the case in mice in which auditory cortical input to the midbrain had been removed by bilateral cortical lesions. This illustrates that subcortical auditory structures have access to a wealth of non-acoustic information and can, independently of the auditory cortex, carry much richer neural representations than previously thought.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental findings showing similar task-related activity in lesioned mice

claim: The animals' behavior can be decoded from the activity of corticorecipient IC shell neurons with a high degree of accuracy.
source: By imaging cellular activity in the corticorecipient shell of the inferior colliculus of mice engaged in a sound detection task, we show that the majority of neurons encode information beyond the physical attributes of the stimulus and that the animals' behavior can be decoded from the activity of those neurons with a high degree of accuracy.
evidence: The claim is supported by the decoding analysis results showing above-chance performance

claim: All experiments were approved by the Committee on Animal Care and Ethical Review at the University of Oxford and were licensed by the UK Home Office.
source: All experiments were approved by the Committee on Animal Care and Ethical Review at the University of Oxford and were licensed by the UK Home Office (Animal Scientific Procedures Act, 1986, amended in 2012).
evidence: The claim is a statement of regulatory compliance

claim: Mice were maintained on a 12 hr light/dark cycle and were housed at 20–24°C with a relative humidity of 45–65%.
source: They were maintained on a 12 hr light/dark cycle and were housed at 20–24°C with a relative humidity of 45–65%.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental housing conditions

claim: Imaging was performed at a depth of 50 μm – 150 μm from the IC surface.
source: Imaging was performed at a depth of 50 μm – 150 μm from the IC surface using a commercial two-photon laser-scanning microscope (B-Scope, ThorLabs, VA, USA)
evidence: The claim describes the experimental imaging parameters

claim: Images were acquired with a resolution of 512 by 512 pixels at a rate of ~28 Hz.
source: Images were acquired with a resolution of 512 by 512 pixels at a rate of ~28 Hz.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental imaging parameters

claim: The size of the field of view was either 500 µm by 500 µm or 666 µm by 666 µm.
source: The size of the field of view was either 500 µm by 500 µm or 666 µm by 666 µm, which allowed us to, typically, image dozens of corticorecipient IC neurons simultaneously.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental imaging parameters
